sections.h2: Where to pay Carter County property tax
sections.html:
County property tax is collected by the Carter County Trustee at the Carter County Courthouse, 801 East Elk Avenue, Elizabethton, TN 37643. The courthouse main number is 423-542-1801. For delinquent tax questions, call 423-542-1811.

You can search and pay bills on citisenportal.com, either with an account or as a guest. An account sends email notices about future bills. If your billing address is wrong, contact the Assessor of Property rather than the Trustee, because the Assessor controls the mailing record.

A house inside Elizabethton owes two taxes, one to the county and one to the city. Rural parcels outside the city limits pay the county bill only. If you are not sure which side of the line a property sits on, ask the Assessor before you assume either way.

sections.h2: Who sets the value of a Carter County house?
sections.html:
The Assessor of Property appraises every parcel. The office is in the courthouse, the phone is 423-542-1801, and email goes to assessor@cartercountytn.gov. The county website links to a real estate assessment data search where you can look up a parcel's appraised value.

A 2026 reappraisal notice is posted on the county site. When a whole county is reappraised, many values shift together and the commission may reset the rate to match. If your number moved, ask the assessor what the new appraisal rests on, and ask the Trustee which rate your 2026 bill uses.

Assessment ratios are set statewide at 25 percent of appraised value for homes and farms and 40 percent for commercial and industrial property. The tax is the assessed value times the rate per $100. Carter County's commission picks the rate each year, typically alongside the budget it adopts near July.

sections.h2: Tax rates for the county and Elizabethton
sections.html:
The county rate is $2.03 and the city rate is $1.57 per $100 of assessed value. Check the current figures with the Trustee, because rates can change in a reappraisal year.

Both bills use the 25 percent residential ratio. Your own parcel's appraisal drives the real number, so pull the current value before you guess at what a buyer will inherit.

County bills open for payment on the first Monday in October and stay interest free through the last day of February. March 1 starts delinquency. Elizabethton keeps a later calendar for its own bills.

  • City notices go out in November.
  • City taxes can be paid without penalty through March 31, 2027, then turn delinquent on April 1, 2027.
  • City payments are taken at the Finance Department, City Hall, 136 S. Sycamore Street, Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.
  • Paying the city by card adds 1.89 percent plus a 50 cent transaction fee.
  • State law bars the city clerk from waiving interest, penalty or court costs.

If you do not receive a notice for each parcel you own in the city, call the property tax clerk at 423-547-6205. Elizabethton describes its notices as a courtesy because state law does not require them, which means a bill that never arrives changes nothing about the deadline.

Your first formal step is the Carter County board of equalization, which usually begins hearing cases June 1 and looks only at the assessor's current-year values. Phone 423-542-1801 to learn where the board meets, to book a time and to get this year's filing cutoff.

Skipping the county board generally forfeits later appeals. If its ruling leaves you unhappy, the next stop is the State Board of Equalization, and you have until August 1 of the tax year or 45 days after the county board mailed its notice, whichever falls later. Separate from appeals, the assessor can fix plain clerical mistakes in coding, ownership, location or physical description before March 1, reaching back to the second year after the tax year at issue.

Gather anything in writing that supports a lower value, like a recent appraisal or the sale price of a similar house nearby, and carry it with you when you book the appointment.

Two other state dates matter for owners with land or rentals. Greenbelt classification applications are due March 15, and exemption applications are due May 20. Owners of business property, including equipment in a rental business, receive personal property schedules by February 1 and should return them by March 1.

sections.h2: Tax relief for elderly, disabled and veteran owners
sections.html:
A state program repays some or all of the local tax for low-income elderly and disabled owners, plus disabled veteran owners and their surviving spouses. You still get the bill and pay it first, so it works as a refund, not an exemption. Only a primary residence counts.

Forms are handed out at the county Trustee's office and at the city's collecting office. Elizabethton adds a condition: unpaid city taxes from earlier years end eligibility. Anyone counting on relief should make sure every prior year is settled before putting the house on the market.

Once taxes are over 13 months past due, payment goes through the Clerk and Master at 423-542-1812, and that office also conducts tax sales. To get a payoff on a delinquent parcel, begin with the Trustee at 423-542-1811.

Elizabethton's guidance on sales is blunt. If a closing happens after January 1, the owner of record on that date still gets the bill, and the settlement statement should charge the seller's pro-rata portion. The tax is a lien on the land itself, so a buyer carries the job of confirming earlier years were paid.

In practice, the order of work looks like this:

  • Ask the Trustee for the county balance and the city Finance Department for the city balance.
  • Give both figures to the title company so they appear on the settlement statement.
  • Pay any prior-year balance at closing out of the proceeds.
  • Split the current year between buyer and seller by the dates each party owns the house.

A buyer who pays cash and closes quickly still wants clean tax records, so having the payoff figures ready before you accept an offer saves days.

sections.h2: Carter County housing at a glance
sections.html: The county counts about 57,361 residents and 28,715 housing units, with owners living in 75.2 percent of homes. Most buyers and sellers here are dealing with an owner-occupied house, so relief programs and the two-bill setup inside Elizabethton come up often.

faqs.q: Where do I pay Carter County property taxes?
faqs.a: Take the county share to the Trustee at 801 East Elk Avenue in Elizabethton, or use citisenportal.com. A house inside the city also owes the city, which collects at City Hall, 136 S. Sycamore Street.

faqs.q: What is the deadline for Elizabethton city property tax?
faqs.a: The last day to pay 2026 city taxes without penalty is March 31, 2027. They become delinquent on April 1, 2027.

faqs.q: How do I find out what my Carter County home is assessed at?
faqs.a: Phone the Assessor of Property at 423-542-1801, or try the real estate assessment data link on the county assessor page. Homes are assessed at 25 percent of the appraised figure.

faqs.q: Who handles delinquent Carter County taxes?
faqs.a: The Trustee handles delinquent questions at 423-542-1811. Taxes more than 13 months past due go through the Clerk and Master at 423-542-1812, which also runs tax sales.

faqs.q: Do I still owe tax if I get state tax relief?
faqs.a: Yes. Relief is a state reimbursement, not an exemption. You receive the bill, pay it, and the state repays all or part of the taxes paid.
